content: A stillbirth, also referred to as quiet birth, occurs when a fetus that has died in the uterus or during labor and delivery is expelled from the mother’s body. This term is distinct from live birth or miscarriage. Most stillbirths happen in full-term pregnancies. Some sources define stillbirth as the death of a fetus after reaching the mid-second trimester to full-term gestational age. For instance, in the United Kingdom, stillbirth refers to an infant delivered without signs of life after 24 weeks of gestation. In such cases, deaths occurring earlier in pregnancy are often classified as miscarriages. However, other sources use the term stillbirth regardless of the stage of fetal development. The causes of many stillbirths remain unknown, even after extensive testing and autopsy. This phenomenon is sometimes referred to as Sudden Antenatal Death Syndrome (SADS). When the cause is identifiable, potential factors include bacterial infections, birth defects, chromosomal abnormalities, growth retardation, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, maternal diabetes or hypertension, maternal use of nicotine, alcohol, recreational drugs (excluding cannabis), or contraindicated pharmaceutical drugs, postdate pregnancy, placental abruption, physical trauma, radiation poisoning, Rh disease, and umbilical cord accidents. A decrease or cessation in fetal movement may indicate fetal distress or death. However, it is not uncommon for a healthy fetus to exhibit reduced movement, particularly near the end of pregnancy when space in the uterus becomes limited. Nonetheless, medical evaluation, including a nonstress test, is recommended if there is any change in the strength or frequency of fetal movements, especially a complete cessation. Many obstetricians and midwives recommend using a kick chart to monitor fetal activity. Fetal distress or death can be confirmed or ruled out through fetoscopy, Doppler ultrasound, standard ultrasound, or electronic fetal monitoring. If the fetus is alive but inactive, special attention is given to the placenta and umbilical cord during ultrasound to ensure there is no compromise in oxygen or nutrient delivery. In cases of in utero fetal death, there is no immediate health risk to the mother, and labor typically begins spontaneously within two weeks. However, after two weeks, the risk of maternal blood clotting complications increases, and induction of labor is recommended. Many women find the emotional burden of carrying a deceased fetus overwhelming and opt for induction. Cesarean delivery is generally not recommended unless complications arise during vaginal delivery. Stillbirth is a relatively common but often random event. In the United States, the average stillbirth rate is approximately 1 in 115 births, equating to around 26,000 stillbirths annually, or one every 20 minutes. In Australia, England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the rate is about 1 in 200 births, while in Scotland, it is 1 in 167. In developing countries, where medical care may be of lower quality or unavailable, the stillbirth rate is significantly higher. In Australia, any stillborn fetus weighing more than 400 grams or more than 20 weeks in gestation must have its birth registered. If the parents later have living children, the stillborn child’s name must be marked with SB when registering the subsequent births. In Canada, the definition of stillbirth was revised in 1959 to align with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) definition of fetal death, established in 1950. In the United Kingdom, stillbirths must be registered by law. The Stillbirth Definition Act (1992) defines a stillbirth as any child expelled from its mother after the 24th week of pregnancy that did not breathe or show any other signs of life. In England and Wales, registration must occur within 42 days, and a Stillbirth Certificate is issued to the parents. In Scotland, registration must occur within 21 days. In the United States, there is no standardized definition of stillbirth. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) collects data on live births, fetal deaths, and induced terminations of pregnancy from 57 reporting areas, each with its own guidelines and definitions. Many areas do not use the term stillbirth at all. Federal guidelines suggest that fetal death and stillbirth can be used interchangeably. The CDC defines fetal death based on the WHO’s 1950 definition. Federal guidelines recommend reporting fetal deaths with a birth weight over 350 grams or those occurring after 19 weeks of gestation. Forty-one areas use a definition similar to the federal one, thirteen use a shortened definition, and three have no formal definition of fetal death. Only eleven areas specifically use the term stillbirth, with varying criteria regarding gestational age or weight constraints.
